## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.65845.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.65845.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

In this study, Updegrove et al., determined how and why the key sporulation protein SpoIVA from Bacillus subtilis evolved from an ancestral enzyme with GTPase activity towards the ATPase it is nowadays. The authors identified changes in active site amino acids that accomplished the change in nucleotide specificity. An engineered SpoIVA variant functioned as GTPase but failed to polymerize, suggesting an important role of the nucleotide base in this biological function. The authors propose that increased ATP relative to GTP levels at the end of sporulation drove the evolutionary conversion of SpoIVA towards its novel nucleotide preference.

Decision letter after peer review:

[Editors’ note: the authors submitted for reconsideration following the decision after peer review. What follows is the decision letter after the first round of review.]

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Resurrection of ancestral GTPase activity in an extant ATPase reveals a nucleotide base requirement for function" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by a Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Peter Setlow (Reviewer #2).

Our decision has been reached after consultation between the reviewers. Based on these discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife.

Indeed, while all of us thought that your study addresses an interesting research question and that the mutagenesis and general characterization of the mutant proteins was well performed, the expert reviewers identified several shortcomings in your study. These shortcomings were on one hand related to missing experimental data that seem essential to support the conclusions of your manuscript and on the other hand the somewhat biased experimental setup.

While ancestor resurrection can be a powerful approach to provide insights into protein evolution and specialization, your study was not considered to follow the usual approaches that allow the identification of ancestral proteins. Indeed, your exclusive focus on the active site of SpoIVA could have biased your study, as such a targeted analysis ignores the periphery of the nucleotide binding site and the co-evolving protein as a whole (e.g., more commonly used resurrection approaches are based on phylogeny and statistical methods).

In addition, the lack of mechanistic insight regarding the biochemical differences between SpoIVA and SpoIVA-resurrected as well as lack of mechanistic insight of the oligomerization step makes it difficult to conclude that the different nucleotide bases cause this effect compared to other possibilities (e.g., lower ATPase activity, other changes introduced by the mutations, whether similar ATPase-dependent intermediates are observable or not, etc).

The experts also missed experiments with ADP/GDP, non-hydrolyzing analogues of ATP and GTP (e.g. ATPgammaS or GTPgammaS), and potentially also transition state analogues, which seems to be essential to distinguish between conformational changes/protection from proteolysis versus merely nucleotide binding.

Lastly, it was noted that a primary argument used in your manuscript for the change in NTP preference (from GTP to ATP) is based on a drop in the GTP levels after the onset of sporulation. However, the published data on this aspect seem to have addressed a time point of max. 2 hr after sporulation induction, which might be before SpoIVA's function. Getting definitive data for levels of ATP/GTP in the sporulating cell at around the time that SpoIVA is active would therefore be crucial to support your central argument. While the reviewers appreciate that these experiments are not trivial, definitive data on this point using current technology could be important not only for this manuscript but for the sporulation field as a whole.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, Updegrove and colleagues investigated the role of ATP versus GTP hydrolysis in the oligomerization of SpoIVA during B. subtilis sporulation. Authors form the same group previously showed that SpoIVA contains a TRAFAC class GTPase domain that uses ATP hydrolysis rather than GTP hydrolysis to perform its function. They further previously showed that ATP hydrolysis rather than ATP binding is required to induce conformational changes in the SpoIVA subunit that drive incorporation into nucleotide-free SpoIVA polymeric filaments. In the current study the authors re-engineered the binding pocket of SpoIVA toward the (presumed) ancestral counterpart displaying equal catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) toward ATP and GTP. Interestingly they find that, unlike ATP hydrolysis, GTP hydrolysis does not support SpoIVA polymerization in vitro. This indicates that apparently also the nucleotide base plays a role in protein function, rather than just the energy release from phosphodiester bond hydrolysis. Although this is a very interesting finding per se, mechanistic insights regarding either the processes leading to protein oligomerization or the presumed role of the nucleotide base in this process are rather limited. I also have a number of questions and doubts regarding the experimental support for some of the claims that are being made, as outlined below.

1) It is not entirely clear to me what the added value is of the re-engineering toward an ancestral protein with equal kcat/KM values for GTP and ATP for the final conclusions. Wild-type SpoIVA displays only a relatively marginal preference (somewhat more than three-fold) for ATP over GTP? Moreover, wild-type SpoIVA in fact uses GTP more efficiently than the resurrected SpoIVA. Why didn't the authors just use wild-type SpoIVA to show that GTP does not induce polymerization in vitro?

2) In Figure 2—figure supplement 1 the Michaelis-Menten curves for GTP and ATP hydrolysis are shown. Also, the resulting kcat and KM values should be reported (rather than just kcat/KM).

From the curves it seems that the KM values for ATP and GTP hydrolysis are rather severely affected for the resurrected SpoIVA (NSxD SxA), potentially leading to a large error on the fitted parameters (due to saturation not being reached). Under these circumstances one can also doubt how much of the protein is being bound under the substrate conditions used in most other experiments (generally 4 mM ATP or GTP is used which seems to be not saturating for ATP).

3) Subsection “ATP, but not GTP, hydrolysis drives in vitro polymerization of resurrected SpoIVA” and Figure 4A/B. The authors make the observation that mutants NKxR SxE, NKxD SxE, NKxD AxA are not able to utilize the energy released from hydrolysis of either ATP or GTP to drive conformational changes in the protein. This while these mutants hydrolyze ATP or GTP equally well, and even better, than wild-type SpoIVA. This observation is both rather strange and intriguing. However, to prove that the conformational change and protection from proteolysis is really due to hydrolysis and not merely to nucleotide binding, it is required that this experiment is also performed in presence of ADP/GDP, non-hydrolyzing analogues of ATP and GTP (e.g. ATPgammaS or GTPgammaS), and potentially also transition state analogues such as ADP.AlFx and GDP.AlFx.

Related to the remark above: the experiments shown in Figure 4A are done with 4 mM ATP or GTP and thus under multiple turnover conditions. This means that every enzyme molecule presumably went through subsequent rounds of substrate turnover. The main nucleotide state the protein resides in at any particular moment would thus depend on the relative rate of substrate binding, chemical turnover and product release. Could the authors comment on the main nucleotide state SpoIVA would be in during limited proteolysis?

4) Subsection “Formation of an ADP-bound SpoIVA multimeric intermediate is required for polymerization”. The authors report that addition of ATP to SpoIVA, below its critical concentration of polymerization, resulted to a shift of the peak on SEC toward the void volume.

– This seems to contradict what was reported in Castaing et al., 2013, where the authors (from the same group) report that "presence or absence of ATP did not affect the oligomerization state of IVA" at a concentration of 2µM.

– The SEC-MALS experiment should also be performed in presence of ADP (and preferentially a non-hydrolysable ATP analogue, which differs from the strategy of using a protein variant where one of the main crucial switch residues has been mutated!).

– Subsection “Formation of an ADP-bound SpoIVA multimeric intermediate is required for polymerization” and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C: In the SEC-MALS experiment the authors find a peak (see above) in the void volume, and the MALS analysis reveals a varying range of molecular masses ranging from 10E6 to 5.10E3 kDa. The authors interpret this as "at least 36 monomers" and in Figure 7 this becomes ∼ 16 dimers. Using a subunit molecular mass of 57kDA, a quick calculation shows that the peak would contain species ranging between 35 and about 15000 subunit copies, which might just as well correspond to aggregates rather than an "on-pathway" intermediate. The authors could for example use (negative stain) EM to investigate the nature of the species in the void volume and make that distinction.

Reviewer #2:

This paper describes work on the SpoIVA protein essential for spore coat assembly during sporulation of the bacterial spore-former Bacillus subtilis. SpoIVA uses ATP hydrolysis to drive its polymerization on the outside of the developing spore, providing a framework for coat assembly. However, SpoIVA appears to have evolved from an ancestor that preferentially used GTP not ATP. The authors have made multiple amino acid changes in residues involved in NTP hydrolysis/recognition, converting present SpoIVA to a protein using GTP as well as ATP – at least in vitro. The catalytic efficiency of the wt and ultimate mutant (SpoIVAresurrected) protein in vitro, was ~4-fold higher with ATP than GTP for wt SpoIVA but ~1 for SpoIVAresurrected. This difference is likely bigger in vivo since intracellular [ATP] is ~ 5-fold higher than [GTP]. Since [GTP] is reported to fall significantly in sporulation, the authors suggest that this factor is what drove the evolution of SpoIVA to preferentially use ATP.

The authors' mutagenesis, analyses of wt and mutant proteins' ATP and GTP hydrolysis in vitro at different [NTP], in vitro polymerization of proteins with either NTP, and sporulation efficiency with the wt, resurrected strain and other mutants all seems well done. Surprisingly, the resurrected SpoIVA protein completely complemented sporulation of a spoIVA mutant.

1) Following all the data in the ms and drawing conclusions was difficult since there was no Table summarizing mutants' behavior in vivo and in vitro. It was also difficult to assess the likely preference of ATP/GTP in vivo, as presumably the catalytic efficiencies reported for the variants in vitro is at saturating [ATP] and [GTP] and in vivo [GTP] is usually ~5-fold lower than [ATP] and presumably much less early in sporulation (see #2). Overall, it was not easy to see why SpoIVA likely preferred ATP over GTP in sporulation for both the wt and resurrected strain. A Table summarizing various properties of various SpoIVA proteins in vitro and in vivo would be helpful to the reader.

2) The basis for suggesting that low GTP levels in sporulation drove changes in NTP preference in SpoIVA is work from Ernst Freese years ago that showed significant drops in [GTP] upon sporulation induction by various conditions, and this may be correct. However, this work reported results only for 2 hr after sporulation induction, and probably before SpoIVA functions. Whether GTP levels are low this late in sporulation is not known. Indeed, since protein and RNA synthesis continue in the mother cell during sporulation, GTP must be continuously available. Unfortunately, there are no analyses of NTPs' levels throughout sporulation.

3) The NTP levels determined by Freese were from culture samples filtered and then the filters floated on formic acid; this took ~8 sec. While values for energy charge (ATP + 0.5 ADP/ATP + AMP + ADP) were what one would have expected for growing bacteria, if GTP turns over more rapidly than ATP, GTP levels determined might be lower than they really are.

Reviewer #3:

In the manuscript, Updegrove et al., use the unique ATPase SpoIVA from Bacillus subtilis as a model to investigate a fundamental question: Does nucleotide identity dictate hydrolysis-driven protein function? In previous work, the authors pointed out that TRAFAC GTPases, and in particular bacterial Era, likely share a common ancestor. SpoIVA is a cytoskeletal protein that uses its ATPase activity to form terminal polymers in an initial step of Bacillus spore formation. Hence, it appears that SpoIVA evolved ATPase activity from a GTPase scaffold to cope with the cellular conditions met during spore formation. Specifically, as the authors argue in the current manuscript, this change may have been driven by limiting GTP concentrations under conditions that drive spore formation, whereas ATP would still be available at higher levels under the same conditions.

To investigate the mechanistic consequences of turning SpoIVA into an Era-like GTPase, targeted mutagenesis at well-established signature motifs that determine substrate preference in these enzymes was employed. One particular mutant, called SpoIVA-resurrected, does not discriminate between ATP or GTP, hydrolyzing both substrates at near-equal efficiency and at efficiencies similar to Era (although with reduced ATPase activity compared to wild-type SpoIVA). In cells, SpoIVA-resurrected supports sporulation at levels similar to wild-type SpoIVA. In tryptic digests, wild-type and "resurrected" SpoIVA are both stabilized by ATP and GTP. For wild-type SpoIVA, polymerization (above a critical protein concentration for polymerization) and an intermediate (below a critical protein concentration) was detected only with ATP. The intermediate was shown to corresponds to an ADP-bound, post-hydrolysis state. Finally, it was shown that SpoIVA-resurrected has comparatively reduced sensitivity to ATP concentrations, with wild-type SpoIVA polymerizing at much lower ATP levels.

While the work addresses a fundamental question, major concerns regarding the approach used to investigate the evolution of functional specialization of GTPases and ATPases dampen enthusiasm for this study. Also, the molecular mechanism responsible for the biochemical differences between SpoIVA and SpoIVA-resurrected remains enigmatic, which, together with alternative explanations for the apparent differences in polymerzation and other caveats, may limit the perceived impact.

1) Ancestor resurrection has become a popular method for rationalizing the evolution of structural and/or functional properties in related proteins. Usually, the approach involves statistical methods to predict the evolution of proteins or domains based on phylogeny, taking into account conservation across their entire sequence. Here, the authors focus exclusively on functional motifs in the active site of SpoIVA (and Era). This is a fairly targeted analysis that does not take into account residues in the periphery of the nucleotide binding site (or the protein as a whole) that could contribute to substrate specificity, catalytic efficiency, and/or switching. One concern is that by doing so, the authors may miss residues or regions in the protein, which may co-evolve with the active-site motifs, shaping the functional properties of the entire protein.

It is recommended to use one of the now common approaches to resurrect the last common ancestor of SpoIVA and Era (see e.g. 10.1146/annurev-biophys-070816-033631), and study its properties in an unbiased fashion (e.g., What sequence motifs emerge? What is its activity and substrate profile? Does it polymerize and/or form hydrolysis-dependent oligomers?).

2) The authors use Era, "ancestral Era GTPase", and the ancestor interchangeably (e.g., subsection “The altered NKxD motif in G4 and SxE sequence in G5 mediate nucleotide specificity of SpoIVA”, but common throughout the manuscript). However, Era appears to be an extant enzyme that likely evolved independently after the emergence of SpoIVA, which may have further contributed to the specialization of the two proteins compared to a common ancestor. Careful separation between extant Era and SpoIVA and predicted common ancestors would avoid the potential for confusion.

3) If the targeted changes in the primary active site motifs fully recapitulate the evolutionary and functional differences between SpoIVA and Era, one may predict that the corresponding changes in Era would result in SpoIVA-like properties. This would be a crucial experiment to consider for this study.

4) While the type of mutations introduced into SpoIVA was guided by sequence comparison with Era-type GTPases, it appears that the authors chose the mutant they refer to as the resurrected ancestor based on the activity profile that matches most closely the catalytic characteristics of Era, and not necessarily based on the phylogenic analysis. This practice introduces bias that may hamper the analysis concerning the evolution of substrate specificity.

In this context, it is also not clear why the authors assume that the last common ancestor of SpoIVA and Era had Era-like hydrolysis efficiencies and substrate preference.

5) The authors also did not consider the potential impact the register shift in G5 between SpoIVA (sequence SxE) and Era (sequence SA) may have, only focusing on the sequence register found in SpoIVA. It is conceivable that the additional residue in this motif arose to accommodate an ATP preference and ATPase-driven mechanism.

6) It is not clear whether the defects in polymerization characteristics of the SpoIVA-resurrected mutant can be attributed to the lower ATPase activity compared to wild-type SpoIVA (or other subtle changes introduced by the mutations). It is also not clear whether SpoIVA-resurrected forms a similar ATPase-dependent intermediate that was oberserved with wild-type SpoIVA (at protein concentrations below the threshold for polymerization). This is an important experiment since the differences between ATP and GTP in their capacity to drive intermediate formation could be explained by the different ATPase vs GTPase efficiencies of the wild-type protein; SpoIVA-resurrected has overall lower catalytic activity compared to wild-type, and it does not support polymerization. Hence, there is a possibility that the observed differences can be attributed to catalytic efficiency (maybe in addition to the nature of the nucleotide base).

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the nucleotide measurements in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The Lys in the NKxD motif is consistently substituted by an alcoholic (S/T) residue in the SpoIVA family.
claims.source: The next position is a K in most families of bona fide GTPases (Figure 1A) and the extended sidechain of this lysine forms the 'lateral wall' of the base-binding pocket (Figure 1D). Strikingly, this K is consistently substituted by an alcoholic (S/T) residue in the SpoIVA family.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In SpoIVA, the conserved Asp in the G4 motif is mostly substituted by either of several polar residues, such as K, H, N, or R.
claims.source: The next conserved position in G4 is the D, which is the most important determinant of guanine specificity (Figure 1D). In SpoIVA it is again mostly substituted by either of several polar residues, such as K, H, N, or R.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In SpoIVA, the position corresponding to the conserved S in the G5 motif is less constrained and is usually either N, D, or S.
claims.source: In the case of SpoIVA the position corresponding to the conserved S in the G5 motif is less constrained and is usually either N, D, or S.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: In SpoIVA, two residues downstream of S in the G5 motif, there is a position that is either acidic (D/E) or Q/N in 41% of the orthologs.
claims.source: Two residues downstream of S, there is a position that contributes to the wall of the base-binding pocket. This position is not particularly conserved in TRAFAC GTPases as a whole but in SpoIVA is either acidic (D/E) or Q/N in 41% of the orthologs.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The changes in the G4 (NKxD) and G5 (SxE) regions relative to the bona fide GTPases may have contributed to the emergence of ATP-specificity in SpoIVA.
claims.source: Together, these observations suggested that the changes in the G4 (NKxD) and G5 (SxE) regions relative to the bona fide GTPases may have contributed to the emergence of ATP-specificity in SpoIVA (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from sequence analysis shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Wild-type SpoIVA displayed a catalytic efficiency of 4.2 ± 0.9 min−1 mM−1 for ATP, compared to just 1.3 ± 0.8 min−1 mM−1 for GTP.
claims.source: Wild-type (WT) SpoIVA displayed a catalytic efficiency of 4.2 ± 0.9 min−1 mM−1 for ATP, compared to just 1.3 ± 0.8 min−1 mM−1 for GTP, indicating that the protein hydrolyzed ATP approximately threefold more efficiently than GTP (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Era hydrolyzed GTP with a catalytic efficiency of 0.7 ± 0.2 min−1 mM−1 upon incubation with an RNA oligonucleotide corresponding to the 16S rRNA sequence.
claims.source: By comparison, Era did not display appreciable basal ATPase or GTPase activity, but upon incubation with an RNA oligonucleotide corresponding to the 16S rRNA sequence to which Era binds and which reportedly stimulates the enzymatic activity of Era (Meier et al., 2000; Tu et al., 2011), Era hydrolyzed GTP with a catalytic efficiency of 0.7 ± 0.2 min−1 mM−1, similar to the reported activity of E. coli Era (Tu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Era did not specifically hydrolyze ATP, as evidenced by the failure of the reaction to reach saturation and display Michaelis–Menten kinetics.
claims.source: However, Era did not specifically hydrolyze ATP, as evidenced by the failure of the reaction to reach saturation and display Michaelis–Menten kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J, Figure 2A, 'I.D.' for 'indeterminable').
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claims.claim: Restoring the Asp in the degenerate NKxD motif of SpoIVA did not significantly change the catalytic efficiencies of ATP or GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: Restoring the Asp in the degenerate NKxD motif of SpoIVA did not significantly change the catalytic efficiencies of ATP or GTP hydrolysis but restoring either the Lys or full NKxD motif in SpoIVA resulted in a ~2.5-fold increase in the catalytic efficiency for ATP and ~3.5-fold of that for GTP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Restoring either the Lys or full NKxD motif in SpoIVA resulted in a ~2.5-fold increase in the catalytic efficiency for ATP and ~3.5-fold of that for GTP hydrolysis.
claims.source: Restoring the Asp in the degenerate NKxD motif of SpoIVA did not significantly change the catalytic efficiencies of ATP or GTP hydrolysis but restoring either the Lys or full NKxD motif in SpoIVA resulted in a ~2.5-fold increase in the catalytic efficiency for ATP and ~3.5-fold of that for GTP hydrolysis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Restoring either the single Lys or the full NKxD motif resulted in decreased preference for ATP.
claims.source: Restoring either the single Lys or the full NKxD motif resulted in decreased preference for ATP (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Variants with restored Lys or full NKxD motif displayed an unusually high turnover rate that was ~10-fold higher for both NTPs than that displayed by WT SpoIVA.
claims.source: Curiously, these variants also displayed an unusually high turnover rate that was ~10-fold higher for both NTPs than that displayed by WT SpoIVA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Substituting both the Ser and Glu with Ala in the SxE sequence in the context of the restored NKxD motif resulted in lowered catalytic efficiencies, similar to WT SpoIVA.
claims.source: Substituting both the Ser and Glu with Ala (to disrupt both positions with an amino acid with a short sidechain that is unlikely to perturb overall SpoIVA structure) in the context of the restored NKxD motif resulted in lowered catalytic efficiencies, similar to WT SpoIVA (Figure 2A,C: 'NKxD AxA').
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2A,C.

claims.claim: Changing the SxE sequence to AxA increased the catalytic efficiency of the enzyme for GTP, resulting in drastically reduced specificity for ATP relative to WT SpoIVA.
claims.source: This change also increased the catalytic efficiency of the enzyme for GTP, resulting in drastically reduced specificity for ATP relative to WT SpoIVA (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Combining a restoration of just the Asp residue of the degenerate NKxD motif with disruption of just the Glu of the SxE sequence resulted in an enzyme that displayed a similar catalytic efficiency to that of Era.
claims.source: Finally, combining a restoration of just the Asp residue of the degenerate NKxD motif with disruption of just the Glu of the SxE sequence, resulted in an enzyme that displayed a similar catalytic efficiency to that of Era (Figure 2A, 'NSxD SxA'; hereafter referred to as 'SpoIVAGTPase'; Figure 2C) with a slight preference for GTP over ATP (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The evolved Era variant (EraATPase) hydrolyzed ATP with a catalytic efficiency of 0.2 ± 0.1 min−1 mM−1 upon stimulation with the 16S rRNA fragment.
claims.source: Similar to WT Era, the evolved Era (EraATPase) did not exhibit a basal NTPase activity, but upon stimulation with the 16S rRNA fragment, EraATPase hydrolyzed ATP with a catalytic efficiency of 0.2 ± 0.1 min−1 mM−1 (Figure 2A), but more curiously failed to specifically hydrolyze GTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: EraATPase failed to specifically hydrolyze GTP.
claims.source: Similar to WT Era, the evolved Era (EraATPase) did not exhibit a basal NTPase activity, but upon stimulation with the 16S rRNA fragment, EraATPase hydrolyzed ATP with a catalytic efficiency of 0.2 ± 0.1 min−1 mM−1 (Figure 2A), but more curiously failed to specifically hydrolyze GTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: The Asp of the NKxD motif contributes to nucleotide specificity.
claims.source: The mutational analyses therefore indicate that the Asp of the NKxD motif contributes to nucleotide specificity and that the substitution of Asp to Arg seen in the extant B. subtilis SpoIVA contributes to altering the nucleotide-binding pocket to discriminate against GTP in favor of ATP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The substitution of Asp to Arg in the extant B. subtilis SpoIVA contributes to altering the nucleotide-binding pocket to discriminate against GTP in favor of ATP.
claims.source: The mutational analyses therefore indicate that the Asp of the NKxD motif contributes to nucleotide specificity and that the substitution of Asp to Arg seen in the extant B. subtilis SpoIVA contributes to altering the nucleotide-binding pocket to discriminate against GTP in favor of ATP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The Glu in the SxE sequence contributes to ATP hydrolysis specificity.
claims.source: The Glu in the SxE sequence further contributes to ATP hydrolysis specificity and likely stabilizes the binding of ATP over GTP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Deletion of spoIVA resulted in a >108-fold and a ~106-fold reduction in the production of heat resistant spores and lysozyme-resistant spores, respectively.
claims.source: Deletion of spoIVA resulted in a >108-fold and a ~106-fold reduction in the production of heat resistant spores and lysozyme-resistant spores, respectively (Roels et al., 1992, Figures 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), which could be complemented in trans by the introduction of WT spoIVA at an ectopic chromosomal locus.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Roels et al., 1992.

claims.claim: Expression of the NSxD variant complemented the spoIVA deletion.
claims.source: In contrast, while expression of the NSxD variant (which displayed similar enzymatic activity as WT SpoIVA in vitro; Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2) complemented the spoIVA deletion, complementation by the hyperactive NKxR or NKxD variants resulted in >108-fold and ~104-fold decreases in the production of heat-resistant spores, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Complementation by the hyperactive NKxR or NKxD variants resulted in >108-fold and ~104-fold decreases in the production of heat-resistant spores, respectively.
claims.source: In contrast, while expression of the NSxD variant (which displayed similar enzymatic activity as WT SpoIVA in vitro; Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2) complemented the spoIVA deletion, complementation by the hyperactive NKxR or NKxD variants resulted in >108-fold and ~104-fold decreases in the production of heat-resistant spores, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Mutants that harbored a spoIVA allele containing a full substitution of the SxE sequence (resulting in AxA) largely failed to sporulate when the G4 motif also harbored alterations.
claims.source: Similarly, mutants that harbored a spoIVA allele containing a full substitution of the SxE sequence (resulting in AxA) also largely failed to sporulate when the G4 motif also harbored alterations (Figures 3A and, Supplementary file 2; NKxD AxA and NKxR AxA).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: SpoIVA variants were produced at levels similar to WT SpoIVA.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis of extracts prepared from sporulating cells revealed that these SpoIVA variants were produced at levels similar to WT SpoIVA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: SpoIVAGTPase (NSxD SxA) supported sporulation at near WT levels.
claims.source: Interestingly, SpoIVAGTPase (NSxD SxA), which showed reduced but similar hydrolysis of ATP and GTP (Figure 2), supported sporulation at near WT levels (Figures 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: WT GFP-SpoIVA localized to the surface of the forespore.
claims.source: WT GFP-SpoIVA localized to the surface of the forespore (Figure 3B,B'), as did the NSxD variant which sporulated at near-WT levels (Figure 3C,C').
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3B,B'.

claims.claim: Restoring only the Lys of the degenerate G4 motif or restoring the entire NKxD motif in an otherwise WT SpoIVA resulted in the mis-localization of the variant as a focus near the surface of the forespore.
claims.source: However, restoring only the Lys of the degenerate G4 motif or restoring the entire NKxD motif in an otherwise WT SpoIVA resulted in the mis-localization of the variant as a focus near the surface of the forespore.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3D–F,D'–F'.

claims.claim: Various disruptions to the SxE sequence alone did not abrogate localization of the variant.
claims.source: In contrast, various disruptions to the SxE sequence alone did not abrogate localization of the variant (Figure 3G–I,G'–I').
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3G–I,G'–I'.

claims.claim: SpoIVAGTPase localized similar to WT.
claims.source: Finally, SpoIVAGTPase localized similar to WT (Figure 3J–J'), consistent with its ability to support sporulation at a near-WT level.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3J–J'.

claims.claim: Co-incubation of SpoIVA with either ATP or GTP resulted in a different banding pattern in limited trypsin proteolysis, with full-length protein considerably resistant to degradation even after 10 min.
claims.source: In the absence of nucleotide, SpoIVA was rapidly degraded, resulting in a characteristic banding pattern (Figure 4A). In contrast, co-incubation with either ATP or GTP resulted in a different banding pattern: most noticeably, the full-length protein was considerably resistant to degradation even after 10 min, suggestive of a massive conformational change in the protein upon hydrolysis of either nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A conformational change in WT SpoIVA could be achieved at an approximately similar rate by hydrolysis of either ATP or GTP.
claims.source: The disappearance of full-length SpoIVA was quantified to produce a decay rate which indicated that a conformational change in WT SpoIVA could be achieved at an approximately similar rate by hydrolysis of either by ATP or GTP (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Restoring the Lys alone, the entire NKxD motif alone, or in combination with the entirely disrupted SxE sequence (to AxA) resulted in a rapid decay rate in the presence of either ATP or GTP, indicating that these variants were unable to achieve the characteristic nucleotide-dependent conformational change.
claims.source: In contrast, restoring the Lys alone, the entire NKxD motif alone, or in combination with the entirely disrupted SxE sequence (to AxA) resulted in a rapid decay rate in the presence of either ATP or GTP, indicating that these variants were unable to achieve the characteristic nucleotide-dependent conformational change, consistent with the observed in vivo defects of these variants (Figure 3, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4 and consistent with Figure 3.

claims.claim: Variants harboring substitution of either the Ser or Glu singly or together in the SxE sequence with Ala or SpoIVAGTPase displayed a decay rate in the presence of either nucleotide that was more similar to WT SpoIVA.
claims.source: However, variants harboring substitution of either the Ser or Glu singly or together in the SxE sequence with Ala or SpoIVAGTPase displayed a decay rate in the presence of either nucleotide that was more similar to WT SpoIVA, suggesting that that these variants were able to utilize the energy released from hydrolysis of either ATP or GTP to drive the conformational change in the protein that is a prerequisite for polymerization (Castaing et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4, with citation to Castaing et al., 2013.

claims.claim: WT SpoIVA displayed an intermediate conformational change in the presence of ATP-γ-S or GTP-γ-S, suggesting that the protein bound, but did not hydrolyze, the nucleotide.
claims.source: In the presence of ATP-γ-S or GTP-γ-S, WT SpoIVA displayed an intermediate conformational change suggesting that the protein bound, but did not hydrolyze, the nucleotide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L, M), whereas SpoIVA harboring a Walker A disruption (SpoIVAA*, which prevents ATP binding [Ramamurthi and Losick, 2008]) did not undergo a similar conformational change (Figures 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L, M and Figures 4C,D.

claims.claim: SpoIVA variant harboring a Sensor T disruption (SpoIVAT*) displayed a similar conformational change as WT SpoIVA in the presence of ATP-γ-S and GTP-γ-S.
claims.source: Consistent with this result, the SpoIVA variant harboring a Sensor T disruption (SpoIVAT*, which binds, but does not hydrolyze ATP [Castaing et al., 2013]) displayed a similar conformational change as WT SpoIVA in the presence of ATP-γ-S and GTP-γ-S (Figures 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), and SpoIVAT* binding to ATP.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, with citation to Castaing et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The intermediate conformational change is likely due to nucleotide binding and not due to slow hydrolysis of the bound nucleotide.
claims.source: Together, this suggested that this intermediate conformational change is likely due to nucleotide binding and not due to slow hydrolysis of the bound nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The NKxD variant of SpoIVA displayed a conformational change in the presence of ATP-γ-S and GTP-γ-S similar to SpoIVAA*, suggesting that it did not stably undergo the initial conformational change that occurs upon binding the nucleotide.
claims.source: Interestingly, the NKxD variant of SpoIVA, which exhibited elevated ATP and GTP hydrolysis levels (Figure 2A), displayed a conformational change in the presence of ATP-γ-S and GTP-γ-S similar to SpoIVAA* (Figures 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that it did not stably undergo the initial conformational change that occurs upon binding the nucleotide.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: WT SpoIVA and SpoIVAT* exhibited a similar intermediate conformational change when incubated with ADP or GDP, but not the full conformational change that occurred upon nucleotide hydrolysis.
claims.source: WT SpoIVA and SpoIVAT* exhibited a similar intermediate conformational change when incubated with ADP or GDP, but not the full conformational change that occurred upon nucleotide hydrolysis (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Incubation of WT SpoIVA with either ADP-AlFx or GDP-AlFx produced a conformational change that was similar to that produced upon full hydrolysis of the nucleotide.
claims.source: Curiously, incubation of WT SpoIVA with either ADP-AlFx or GDP-AlFx (Figure 4F) produced a conformational change that was similar to that produced upon full hydrolysis of the nucleotide (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The transition state mimics the activated state facilitated by ATP hydrolysis that is responsible for the conformational change.
claims.source: This suggested that the transition state mimics the activated state facilitated by ATP hydrolysis that is responsible for the conformational change seen in Figure 4A.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Simply binding to ADP or GDP is insufficient to produce the full conformational change in SpoIVA required for polymerization.
claims.source: Taken together, the results suggest that simply binding to ADP or GDP is insufficient to produce the full conformational change in SpoIVA required for polymerization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Hydrolysis of an NTP molecule, while bound to the active site, is required for rearranging SpoIVA into a polymerization-competent state.
claims.source: Instead, hydrolysis of an NTP molecule, while bound to the active site, is required for rearranging SpoIVA into a polymerization-competent state.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Rapid turnover of the bound NTP is incompatible with producing a conformational change required for polymerization.
claims.source: The data are also consistent with a model in which rapid turnover of the bound NTP is incompatible with producing such a conformational change.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Incubation of purified WT SpoIVA with ATP, but not GTP, resulted in a steady increase in hydrodynamic radius over a 5 hr period.
claims.source: Incubation of purified WT SpoIVA, above the critical concentration for polymerization, with ATP, but not GTP, resulted in a steady increase in hydrodynamic radius (Rh) over a 5 hr period, consistent with ATP-dependent polymerization and what we previously observed (Castaing et al., 2013; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Castaing et al., 2013.

claims.claim: WT SpoIVA displayed a greater than ~30% increase in polymerization rate with ATP than GTP.
claims.source: This ratio revealed a greater than ~30% increase in polymerization rate with ATP than GTP (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 2), surprisingly indicating that the conformational change in SpoIVA driven by GTP hydrolysis (Figure 4A,B,E), which appeared similar to the conformational change driven by ATP hydrolysis, did not yield isomers of SpoIVA that were capable of polymerization.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The conformational change in SpoIVA driven by GTP hydrolysis did not yield isomers of SpoIVA that were capable of polymerization.
claims.source: This ratio revealed a greater than ~30% increase in polymerization rate with ATP than GTP (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 2), surprisingly indicating that the conformational change in SpoIVA driven by GTP hydrolysis (Figure 4A,B,E), which appeared similar to the conformational change driven by ATP hydrolysis, did not yield isomers of SpoIVA that were capable of polymerization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Restoring the Asp in the G4 motif only slightly lowered the polymerization rate with ATP.
claims.source: Restoring the Asp in the G4 motif, which did not display any obvious defect in the other assays, only slightly lowered the polymerization rate with ATP (Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: All variants that harbored a restoration of the Lys in the G4 motif were unable to polymerize with either nucleotide.
claims.source: However, all variants that harbored a restoration of the Lys in the G4 motif were unable to polymerize with either nucleotide (Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E; Supplementary file 2), suggesting that substitutions leading to elevated nucleotide hydrolysis were unable to (1) induce a conformational change, (2) were defective in vivo, and (3) were also unable to promote SpoIVA polymerization.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Disruptions to the SxE sequence lowered, but did not abolish, SpoIVA polymerization in the presence of ATP, but none of these variants polymerized in the presence of GTP.
claims.source: Disruptions to the SxE sequence lowered, but did not abolish, SpoIVA polymerization in the presence of ATP, but none of these variants polymerized in the presence of GTP (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-H; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-H.

claims.claim: SpoIVAGTPase only polymerized in the presence of ATP.
claims.source: Likewise, SpoIVAGTPase, which was functional in vivo (Figure 3), and could use either ATP or GTP to induce a similar conformational change after nucleotide hydrolysis (Figure 4A,B), only polymerized in the presence of ATP (Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I; Supplementary file 2), suggesting a specific requirement for the nucleotide base, not simply the energy released from nucleotide hydrolysis, for its function.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: There is a specific requirement for the nucleotide base, not simply the energy released from nucleotide hydrolysis, for SpoIVA function.
claims.source: Likewise, SpoIVAGTPase, which was functional in vivo (Figure 3), and could use either ATP or GTP to induce a similar conformational change after nucleotide hydrolysis (Figure 4A,B), only polymerized in the presence of ATP (Figures 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I; Supplementary file 2), suggesting a specific requirement for the nucleotide base, not simply the energy released from nucleotide hydrolysis, for its function.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Fully polymerized SpoIVA is devoid of any bound nucleotide.
claims.source: Fully polymerized SpoIVA is devoid of any bound nucleotide (Castaing et al., 2013), but we wondered if SpoIVA would form an intermediate multimeric complex en route to polymerization whose formation would be dependent specifically on ADP binding before the hydrolyzed nucleotide was released.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to Castaing et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In the absence of nucleotide or the presence of GTP, SpoIVA migrated as a single peak with a mass of 103 ± 12 kDa, similar to a predicted mass for a SpoIVA dimer of 114 kDa.
claims.source: In the absence of nucleotide or the presence of GTP, SpoIVA migrated as a single peak (Figure 5B, top left; pink and gray traces). Quantitative mass imaging of this peak by employing interferometric scattering mass spectrometry (iSCAMS) (Young et al., 2018) revealed a mass of 103 ± 12 kDa (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), similar to a predicted mass for a SpoIVA dimer of 114 kDa.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, with citation to Young et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Addition of ATP resulted in shifting most of the protein to the void volume of the SEC column, indicating the formation of a larger complex.
claims.source: Addition of ATP resulted in shifting most of the protein to the void volume of the SEC column, indicating the formation of a larger complex (Figure 5B, top left; blue trace), even though the experiment was performed using a SpoIVA concentration that was below its critical concentration for polymerization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Neither SpoIVAT* in the presence ATP or GTP, nor WT SpoIVA in the presence of either ATP-γ-S or ADP, formed a larger complex.
claims.source: In contrast, neither SpoIVAT* in the presence ATP or GTP, nor WT SpoIVA in the presence of either ATP-γ-S or ADP, formed a larger complex, indicating that ATP, but not GTP, hydrolysis is required for producing the species in the void volume (Figure 5B, top right and bottom left).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: ATP, but not GTP, hydrolysis is required for producing the species in the void volume.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Incubation of SpoIVAGTPase with ATP, but not GTP, partially shifted a population into the void volume.
claims.source: Interestingly, incubation of SpoIVAGTPase with ATP, but not GTP, partially shifted a population into the void volume (Figure 5B, bottom right), indicating that the reengineered SpoIVAGTPase retained its specific dependence on ATP instead of GTP in forming the polymerization-competent intermediate, despite being able to hydrolyze both NTPs.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The reengineered SpoIVAGTPase retained its specific dependence on ATP instead of GTP in forming the polymerization-competent intermediate, despite being able to hydrolyze both NTPs.
claims.source: Interestingly, incubation of SpoIVAGTPase with ATP, but not GTP, partially shifted a population into the void volume (Figure 5B, bottom right), indicating that the reengineered SpoIVAGTPase retained its specific dependence on ATP instead of GTP in forming the polymerization-competent intermediate, despite being able to hydrolyze both NTPs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: SEC-MALS analysis revealed a range of molecular weights ranging from 2 × 103 kDa to 106 kDa for the void volume peak, suggesting multimers containing at least ~36 monomers of SpoIVA.
claims.source: Since the mass of the void volume peak was varied and too large to examine using iSCAMS, we employed size exclusion with multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) analysis (Some et al., 2019), which revealed a range of molecular weights ranging from 2 × 103 kDa to 106 kDa, suggesting multimers containing at least ~36 monomers of SpoIVA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, with citation to Some et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Examination of the void volume by negative stain and transmission electron microscopy revealed a species with a distinct structure that extensively self-interacted.
claims.source: Examination of this void volume by negative stain and transmission electron microscopy revealed a species with a distinct structure that extensively self-interacted (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Incubating WT SpoIVA or SpoIVAGTPase with GTP did not reveal a significant absorbance at 254 nm for fractions containing protein.
claims.source: Incubating WT SpoIVA or SpoIVAGTPase with GTP did not reveal a significant absorbance at 254 nm for fractions containing protein (Figure 5C, top left and bottom right; pink traces), but the protein peaks of the sample in the void volume when incubated with ATP displayed significant absorbance at 254 nm (Figure 5C, blue traces), suggesting the presence of nucleotide in this fraction.
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The protein peaks of the sample in the void volume when incubated with ATP displayed significant absorbance at 254 nm, suggesting the presence of nucleotide in this fraction.
claims.source: Incubating WT SpoIVA or SpoIVAGTPase with GTP did not reveal a significant absorbance at 254 nm for fractions containing protein (Figure 5C, top left and bottom right; pink traces), but the protein peaks of the sample in the void volume when incubated with ATP displayed significant absorbance at 254 nm (Figure 5C, blue traces), suggesting the presence of nucleotide in this fraction.

results.result: Sequence analysis reveals that SpoIVA has altered G4 (NKxD) and G5 (SxE) motifs compared to ancestral GTPases. The Lys in the NKxD motif is substituted by Ser/Thr, the conserved Asp is substituted by polar residues (K, H, N, or R), and the G5 motif shows less constrained residues with acidic positions downstream. These changes are proposed to contribute to ATP-specificity in SpoIVA.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 present sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1, documenting specific amino acid substitutions in the G4 and G5 motifs. Claim C38 draws a reasonable inference from this data that these changes may contribute to ATP specificity. The sequence analysis is appropriately documented and the inference is conservative ("may have contributed").

results.result: Mutational analysis of the G4 and G5 motifs demonstrates their roles in nucleotide specificity. Restoring the NKxD motif in SpoIVA increases catalytic efficiency for both ATP and GTP but decreases ATP preference. The SpoIVAGTPase variant (NSxD SxA) displays similar catalytic efficiency to Era with slight GTP preference. Conversely, introducing SpoIVA-like mutations into Era (EraATPase) switches its specificity toward ATP. The Asp in NKxD and Glu in SxE contribute to nucleotide discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C50 present extensive in vitro enzymatic data shown in Figure 2 and supplements, with appropriate replication (n=3-4) and error bars. The Michaelis-Menten kinetics are properly analyzed. Claims C51-C53 draw reasonable mechanistic conclusions from the mutational data. The reciprocal experiments with Era strengthen the conclusions about determinants of nucleotide specificity.

results.result: In vivo complementation assays show that SpoIVA variants with restored Lys or full NKxD motif fail to support sporulation despite being expressed at WT levels. The SpoIVAGTPase variant (NSxD SxA) complements the spoIVA deletion and localizes properly to the forespore surface, supporting near-WT sporulation efficiency. Variants with only SxE disruptions maintain proper localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C63 present in vivo functional data from sporulation assays (Figure 3) and microscopy, with appropriate controls including protein expression levels (C58). The data show clear phenotypic differences between variants, with proper quantification of sporulation efficiency. The localization data by fluorescence microscopy provides additional functional validation. Multiple independent replicates (n=3-4) support the conclusions.

results.result: Limited trypsin proteolysis reveals that both ATP and GTP hydrolysis drive conformational changes in WT SpoIVA at similar rates. Non-hydrolyzable analogs (ATP-γ-S, GTP-γ-S) and ADP/GDP produce only intermediate conformational changes, while transition state mimics (ADP-AlFx, GDP-AlFx) produce full conformational changes. This indicates that NTP hydrolysis while bound to the active site, not simply NDP binding, is required for the polymerization-competent conformational change.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C77 present conformational change data from limited proteolysis assays (Figure 4) with appropriate controls including Walker A and Sensor T mutants. The use of non-hydrolyzable analogs and transition state mimics provides strong mechanistic insight. The data are replicated (n=3-4) and quantified. The conclusions about the requirement for hydrolysis (C75-C77) are well-supported by the systematic analysis of different nucleotide states.

results.result: Dynamic light scattering shows that WT SpoIVA polymerizes with ATP but not GTP, displaying >30% higher polymerization rate with ATP. SpoIVA variants with restored Lys in G4 cannot polymerize with either nucleotide. SpoIVAGTPase, despite undergoing conformational changes with both nucleotides, only polymerizes with ATP, indicating a specific requirement for the ATP base beyond energy release.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 present polymerization data from DLS (Figure 5 and supplements) with appropriate replication (n=3). The systematic analysis of variants correlates with previous enzymatic and conformational data. Claim C85 draws a key mechanistic conclusion that is well-supported by the observation that SpoIVAGTPase hydrolyzes both nucleotides but only polymerizes with ATP, directly demonstrating base-specific requirements beyond energetics.

results.result: Size exclusion chromatography, mass spectrometry, and electron microscopy reveal that ATP hydrolysis drives formation of high molecular weight SpoIVA multimers (2×10³ to 10⁶ kDa) that retain bound ADP. These ADP-bound multimers are functional polymerization intermediates that can polymerize after ATP removal and concentration increase, releasing ADP to form nucleotide-free polymers. GTP hydrolysis does not produce stable multimers or retain GDP.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C105 present a comprehensive characterization of polymerization intermediates using multiple complementary techniques (SEC, iSCAMS, SEC-MALS, EM, UV absorbance). The data clearly show ATP-specific formation of ADP-bound multimers (C87-C98) and their functionality (C99-C102). The model proposed (C103-C105) is well-supported by the experimental evidence. The use of multiple orthogonal methods strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: LC-MS quantification of nucleotides during B. subtilis sporulation shows that ATP levels decrease from 2.3 mM to 1.6 mM at t=3.5h (when SpoIVA assembles) and 0.81 mM at t=5h. GTP drops from 0.65 mM to 0.071 mM immediately upon sporulation induction, then rises to 0.20 mM at t=3.5h, resulting in an ~8-fold ATP:GTP ratio. The alarmones ppGpp and pGpp increase ~30-fold upon sporulation induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C117 present LC-MS metabolomics data (Figure 6A-D) with appropriate replication (n=3) and error bars. The measurements are properly converted to intracellular concentrations using cell volume and detection efficiencies (C110). The data provide important physiological context for understanding the evolutionary pressure for ATP specificity. The alarmone measurements (C116-C117) are consistent with prior literature.

results.result: At physiological nucleotide concentrations (1.5 mM ATP, 0.06 mM GTP), WT SpoIVA undergoes conformational changes and polymerizes efficiently, while SpoIVAGTPase undergoes conformational changes but fails to polymerize. This demonstrates that the extant SpoIVA has evolved to function efficiently at limiting ATP concentrations present during late sporulation, suggesting this was the selective pressure driving nucleotide specificity evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 present functional data at physiologically relevant nucleotide concentrations (Figure 6E-G), directly testing the evolutionary hypothesis. The differential performance of WT vs SpoIVAGTPase at limiting ATP (C120-C121) provides strong support for the evolutionary model. Claim C122 draws a reasonable evolutionary conclusion supported by the combined nucleotide measurement and functional data.

results.result: The authors propose that reduced GTP levels relative to ATP during late sporulation (when SpoIVA functions) provided the evolutionary pressure for SpoIVA to switch from GTP to ATP specificity. This is supported by nucleotide measurements showing 8-fold ATP:GTP excess at t=3.5h, the requirement for low GTP during sporulation, and the superior performance of extant SpoIVA over SpoIVAGTPase at limiting ATP concentrations.
results.evaluation: These claims present the central evolutionary hypothesis, which is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) nucleotide measurements during sporulation (Figure 6A), (2) functional assays at physiological concentrations (Figure 6E-G), (3) literature on GTP depletion during sporulation, and (4) the observation that extant SpoIVA outperforms the ancestral-like variant under physiological conditions. The evolutionary argument is logical and supported by data.

results.result: The authors speculate on the evolutionary trajectory: first, Lys→Ser substitution in the NKxD motif modulated enzyme activity; second, loss of Asp increased ATP preference; finally, emergence of Glu in the G5 loop enhanced ATP catalytic efficiency and polymerization at lower ATP levels. This pathway is supported by the observation that variants retaining Lys are non-functional.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are explicitly speculative ("we can speculate") about the evolutionary pathway. While the speculation is informed by the mutational data showing Lys-containing variants are non-functional (Figures 2-4), this represents a proposed evolutionary trajectory rather than directly tested historical events. The speculation is reasonable but cannot be definitively supported without ancestral reconstruction or additional evolutionary analysis.

results.result: A model is proposed where ATP hydrolysis produces ADP-bound SpoIVA multimers that polymerize upon concentration increase, releasing ADP to form nucleotide-free polymers. GTP hydrolysis fails to retain GDP, preventing multimer formation. This model is consistent with delayed ADP release observed previously and resembles septin GDP-dependent multimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C146 present a mechanistic model (Figure 7) that integrates multiple experimental observations: ADP-bound multimer formation (Figure 5B-C), functional polymerization after ATP removal (Figure 5E-J), nucleotide-free final polymers (C143), and failure with GTP (C146). The model is well-supported by the data and provides a coherent mechanistic framework. The comparison to septins (C142) is appropriate.

results.result: Background claims about nucleotide energetics and typical functions: NTP hydrolysis releases similar energy (~30 kJ/mol), ATP typically powers energy-intensive reactions while GTP functions as a switch, and ATP abundance drove evolution of motor proteins like myosin and kinesin from ancestral GTPases.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C12 present established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations (Berg et al., 2007; Bennett et al., 2009; Leipe et al., 2002). These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims accurately represent current understanding in the field.

results.result: Background on SpoIVA: it is a bacterial cytoskeletal ATPase from the TRAFAC class of GTPases, evolved from Era GTPase via gene duplication, exclusively found in sporulating Firmicutes, essential for spore coat assembly, and requires ATP hydrolysis to form static nucleotide-free polymers. The TRAFAC GTPases contain conserved motifs including the NKxD motif for guanine specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C27 present established background on SpoIVA and TRAFAC GTPases from prior literature (multiple citations to Ramamurthi, Castaing, Leipe, and others). These are well-documented facts that provide essential context. The structural information about the NKxD motif (C25-C27) is supported by crystal structure data from the literature.

results.result: Literature-based claims about GTP depletion: amino acid starvation and stationary phase reduce GTP/GDP levels while increasing (p)ppGpp, GTP depletion is implicated in sporulation initiation, (p)ppGpp inhibits GTP production, and artificially elevating GTP during nutrient limitation is detrimental.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126, C129-C130 present established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations (Kriel et al., 2012; Lopez et al., 1979; Ochi et al., 1982). These provide important physiological context for understanding the selective pressure for ATP specificity but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: Discussion claims about functional implications: SpoIVA retained the ancestral 'switch' function of GTPases (conformational change upon hydrolysis), was likely recruited for structural roles due to GTPase oligomerization capacity, and functionally resembles STAND clade ATPases that use ATP hydrolysis to transmit conformational changes rather than perform motor functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C152 present interpretive conclusions about SpoIVA's functional evolution. C148 is well-supported by the conformational change data (Figure 4). C149 is reasonable speculation based on GTPase properties. C151-C152 make appropriate comparisons to STAND clade proteins with proper citations (Leipe et al., 2004; Danot et al., 2009). These provide useful functional context.

results.result: Summary claims from abstract: SpoIVAGTPase functions as a GTPase but fails to polymerize due to inability to form an NDP-bound intermediate required for polymerization. It also fails to polymerize efficiently with limiting ATP. This reveals that the nucleotide base, beyond energy release, is critical for function, and ATP abundance during late sporulation drove the evolutionary change.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C30-C32 are summary statements from the abstract that accurately reflect the major findings presented in the manuscript. They are supported by the detailed experimental data in Figures 2-6, including enzymatic assays, conformational change studies, polymerization assays, and nucleotide measurements. These represent appropriate high-level summaries of the work.
